title: the birth of the cousins
hook: a forest sage with blazing eyes comes to a palace bedroom, a frightened widow shuts her eyes, and a son is born blind
carry: a widow too frightened to look

segments.voice: Last week ended with Satyavati thinking of her firstborn, and Vyasa appearing at once. She thinks of him; he comes.

Vyasa comes to the palace straight from the forest, and he looks it. The text describes him: dark skin, matted hair the color of copper, a rough beard, blazing eyes, and a smell no one would call perfume. His mother has asked him to give the house of the Kurus a son. He agrees, and asks that they wait first. Satyavati answers: there is no time.
screen: `A SAGE FROM THE FOREST.` → `HE ASKS FOR TIME.` → `THERE IS NO TIME.`

segments.voice: This begins a new part: the birth of the cousins. First the fathers are born, then the cousins who will one day face each other across a battlefield. It starts with an ancient custom: when a man died without children, a learned man could be invited to father them in his name, so the line would go on. Vyasa says the widows should first keep a vow, to be ready. Satyavati says the kingdom can't wait for a king. So Vyasa says: then let the princess bear my looks, my smell, my grim face. That will be her vow. Satyavati tells the elder widow, Ambika, that a brother-in-law will come to her tonight. Ambika thinks of the heroes of the Kuru house, and waits. The lamp is lit, and in comes Vyasa, with his blazing eyes and copper hair. She's afraid, and she shuts her eyes, and keeps them shut. Afterward Vyasa tells his mother: the son will be strong and wise, a fine prince. But because his mother closed her eyes, he will be born blind. Satyavati answers at once: a blind man can't be king of the Kurus. Give the family another. That son is Dhritarashtra. Vyasa ties the blindness to Ambika's closed eyes, but the text doesn't make her a villain. It shows a widow too frightened to look, a mother in a hurry, and a son who will spend his life near a throne he can't fully have.

segments.voice: Ambika closed her eyes because she was afraid. Bring to mind something you've been not looking at, a bill, a conversation, a feeling, and without opening it, turn toward it a little, the way you'd turn toward a sound in the next room. Notice the fear, if it's there, and breathe beside it.
Dhritarashtra, born blind because his mother, Ambika, couldn't bear to look at the sage who fathered him.
Your line: a widow too frightened to look. One night's fear shaped a whole life. See you tomorrow.
